entries.title: The best books on The Panama Canal, recommended by Julie Greene
entries.summary: The Panama Canal was an engineering feat but also a social feat, coordinating tens of thousands of workers, uprooting their families, and displacing a former world in the heart of Panama. Historian Julie Greene picks five books to tell the story of Panama from every angle - from the early attempts to the economic outcomes, via the extraordinary lives of the men and women who made it possible. entries.content:
The Panama Canal was an engineering feat but also a social feat, coordinating tens of thousands of workers, uprooting their families, and displacing a former world in the heart of Panama. Historian Julie Greene picks five books to tell the story of Panama from every angle - from the early attempts to the economic outcomes, via the extraordinary lives of the men and women who made it possible.

Let’s begin at the beginning: why was the Panama Canal built?

The idea of building a canal across the Isthmus of Panama had been a dream for centuries. Traffic otherwise had to go around the southern tip of South America, which made the trip thousands of miles longer.

The first step was a railroad built in the 1850s, the first transcontinental railroad in the Western Hemisphere. Then the French tried and failed, tragically and infamously. Then the US tried. The US, in addition to wanting to avoid that long trip, saw it as useful for a range of economic and military reasons. It was sparked by the so-called Spanish-American War, during which it took a long time for the US Navy to travel around that southern tip.

It was also a time when Theodore Roosevelt, as president, had great ambitions for the US. He wanted the US to become a global power commensurate with Europe, and saw military and naval power in particular as key to that.

High stakes. On to your first choice: tell us about The Path Between the Seas, by David McCullough.

This is still by far the most widely read book about the Canal’s history, and it has a lot of strengths. It won several prizes for good reason. McCullough is a wonderful writer, and he brings forward a sweeping pageant of life. It has a broad chronology: it covers both the French and the US construction efforts. So, there’s good reason why it’s still so widely read today.

It is, by the standards of the other books I’ll talk about, rather triumphalist in the way it sees US power in the Canal Zone, and the importance of the Canal. Theodore Roosevelt would read the book and think it beautifully expressed his view: that this was not about imperialism, but was a gift to global civilization based on American strength in medicine, engineering, technology, etc.

It’s definitely a great book to read. Many people who are taking a cruise through the Canal think of it first, and it’s a great contrast to the other books that we’ll talk about.

As I understand it from your own book, a triumphalist narrative was not unanimously shared at the time it was being built…

Yes – and McCullough covers that. He has a wonderful eye for the ironies of history. So when I say it’s triumphalist, I don’t mean that he completely erases the downsides. He certainly discusses the ways in which it was a pretty naked grab by the United States, for example…

Tell us more.

The United States wanted the Canal and tried to negotiate with Colombia – Panama at that time was a part of Colombia. Colombia refused, so the United States let it be known among Panamanians that the US would support a revolt, and sent warships. Then when the revolt happened, the US immediately negotiated a treaty that gave it permanent and complete control, “as if it were sovereign”, over the Panama Canal Zone. So this young country, at its birth, had the entire heart of its country taken away from it.

Let’s start digging into these contrasting stories. Your second choice is Dying to Better Themselves, by Olive Senior. Could you introduce us?

Olive Senior is Jamaican, best known for her poetry and novels, so she came to this task—a nonfiction book focused on Caribbean workers—with these incredible writing skills. So first of all, it’s just a really beautiful narrative. She integrates cultural sources like songs and fictional writings into how she understands the Caribbean people.

She centres the Caribbean itself in this story: she shows how the building of the Canal, and the vast migrations across the Caribbean that made it possible, reshaped not only Panama but the Caribbean too. In addition, like McCullough, she covers a broader chronology. She begins with Caribbean migration during the construction of the railroad in the 1850s, goes through the French Canal project, and then through the US project; so it gives us a longer context for understanding the relationship between the Caribbean and the Canal. And finally, she moves the chronology forward as well, following what happened when the Canal was finished: migration back home or permanent settlement in Panama.

Throughout all of that, she takes this group – the Caribbean, mostly male labour force that we think we know – and she shows us the complexity of it: the ways they accommodated themselves to the power of the United States and to life in Panama or the Zone, and the ways they resisted. It’s a beautiful book that marked new approaches to thinking about the history of the Canal.

It’s maybe worth underscoring here what a huge part of the workforce we’re referring to – I believe you wrote that over 30,000 out of the 62,000-strong population of the Zone were from the Caribbean. Could we talk about this link? The US was actively recruiting there, right?

Right. They went to the Caribbean because people there were English speaking, and they were thought to be more easily disciplined. They tended not to use the local workers, so there were relatively few Panamanians, only a few thousand.

The workforce was very hierarchical. There was the so-called ‘unskilled labour’, which was Caribbean workers; and then ‘skilled labour’ was predominantly white US workers, and a few thousand Europeans as well. For a while, they brought in Spaniards and Italians and Greeks, thinking they might help push the Caribbean workers to work harder.

Your next choice takes us to a more hidden world of labour: tell us about Joan Flores-Villalobos’s The Silver Women: How Black Women’s Labour Made The Panama Canal.

Yes, as you say, this takes us to the work and the world of Caribbean women. Much of the work that’s been done by McCullough, and even by Senior, has tended to give less attention to women. The sources are harder to find on the Caribbean women; it’s much more of a hidden world. Joanne Flores Villalobos had to tease out the information from creative use of sources.

She also came to it wanting to understand different things. She framed the book as focused on social reproduction, the work that women did to make it possible for the work on the Canal to happen: the work of feeding, caring for the sick, housing… All of that work becomes important in her story.

Along the way, she shows that understanding women more fully changes our entire understanding of the project. They shaped the economy, and like the male labourers, they had to choose between accommodating themselves to the power of the US or resisting – typically, of course, doing some of both. They negotiated wages; they fought for more respect; they went to court over insults issued against them. They fought to get money from husbands or domestic partners who abandoned them. One of the most common jobs they had was in the home of a white US housewife, so she also shows us how empire shapes intimate relations by zooming in on how these women interacted with their bosses.

Official policy did not at first encourage women joining, right?

Yes, that is a really interesting part of it. The US thought it would be too messy and complicated to have women there, whether from the US or from the Caribbean. There’s a story that I’ve never been able to find the actual evidence for, that the reason the US relented and started allowing women to come was that the Caribbean workers had a sit-down strike and said, “No women, no work” – and then the white workers did the same thing.

The Canal project started in 1904, and by 1908-9 there were thousands of women there – both white housewives from the US, and Caribbean women who came for much the same reasons as their menfolk did. They came sometimes to support their men and make sure they had someone who would cook for them, but also to escape the hardships of their home islands, Jamaica or Barbados. And sometimes because they wanted some adventure, and thought they could make more money building the Yankees’ Canal.

Could we quickly explain the title, ‘The Silver Women’ – I assume a reference to the silver and gold system?

Yes. Really crucial to the whole Canal project was the silver and gold system, which was a biracial system in which white workers were paid in gold and other workers, mostly Caribbean, in silver. It’s in many ways comparable to Jim Crow in the United States. It was not just different kinds of currency: the gold workers were treated much better. They had six weeks’ vacation, and they made more money than they would in the US. The silver workers lived in shacks that lacked screens, were much more susceptible to disease and accidents, and were paid much less. In talking about the ‘silver women’, Flores is broadening out from just the currency system, since the majority of these women weren’t actually part of the silver-gold system. She’s looking at the broader significance of the segregation system, and how women responded to it.

All of this circles something fascinating about the Canal: that it didn’t just require engineering feats, but also the creation of a whole autonomous district with tens of thousands of people, which had to be built up in ten years, governed, and then dismantled again. That world is presented in amazing detail in your own book The Canal Builders: could you introduce your project there?

I came to the topic as a labour historian, interested also in issues of race and gender and migration. All of these were things that McCullough dealt with relatively little. I wanted to show that the labour problem in the Canal was really at the heart of the project. We often think of it as a triumph of engineering and medicine, and certainly, that’s how McCullough saw it. But, from the beginning, I took some wisdom from the chief engineer of the project, George Washington Goethals. He said that those aspects really weren’t that innovative. What was innovative was figuring out how to discipline and manage this vast workforce of people – so that’s what The Canal Builders took on.

The book is incredibly rich in personal stories. Could we talk a little about the archives you used?

Yes – the sources are phenomenal, especially from the perspective of it being a United States project. The best place for information about it is the records of the US government held at the National Archives. The government obsessively recorded every single detail. Beyond that, there are records in Panama that helped me understand the project from a Panamanian perspective, and there are records in the United Kingdom, because the Caribbean labourers were colonial subjects of the British Empire, and the British were keeping an eye on them. They would often write to their diplomatic representatives in the UK, and those letters were some of the very best sources I found in terms of the Caribbean experience and perspective.

When I began the project, I thought I was just going to focus on the white skilled workers who went to the canal, and I figured McCullough’s book had probably done it all. But the minute I got into the sources, I saw that the things that interested me were such a small part of his book: how people lived, how people worked, what forms of exploitation they experienced, and how they responded to or reacted against them. There were voluminous sources that brought that part of the story to life. In my very first visit to the National Archives, I realised that there was a book here, the sort of book that I would want to write.

Then I knew I had to go to Panama and see what was there. And a friend of mine who had done work at Kew, at the UK’s National Archives, said, ‘I think no historian working on the Canal has ever visited that archive, but I think you’ll find a lot there…’ So towards the end of my research, I took the plunge and went, and it was a final gold mine.

I loved the details from the letters to consuls. The court records were astonishing too…

Yes. No one had ever looked at those, and I remember searching and searching for where they might be, and it turned out they were here in D.C. at the National Archives. They were incredible – the criminal suits and the prison labour issues, but also the civil records. For example, one of the best ways I traced women’s experiences was looking at the divorce records. The white US men would ask their wives to come join them in Panama – some working-class carpenter’s wife in Detroit, or something – and a lot of wives would say, ‘Hell no, I’m not going to the wilderness that is Panama.’ And then the men would divorce them on grounds of abandonment, because at that time the law said that if you don’t go where your husband wants you to go, you’ve abandoned him. So they divorced their wives, and married some young Panamanian woman, and both the wife and husband would enter letters between them as evidence, going back sometimes years and years. That let me document these marriages, and the lives of working-class men and women. It was really fascinating – a whole world I had no idea about.

Really interesting. Ok, your fourth choice is going to carry the story on beyond the building years: this is Noel Maurer and Carlos Yu’s The Big Ditch: How America Took, Built, Ran, and Ultimately Gave Away the Panama Canal.

I include this book partly because it’s just so different from the others. It’s a little more dry – it’s an economic history of the canal, where the other books we’re talking about lean more towards social history. Maurer and Yu quantitatively and qualitatively examine the economic impact of an imperial project like the Panama Canal. Did it make money? Who did it make money for? How did that change over time?

What they found was really interesting. At first, the Canal’s advantages could be seen pretty clearly. It obviously made traffic cheaper; it saved thousands of miles, etc. But they found that while those improvements helped the global economy, they didn’t really benefit the United States government itself. Furthermore, what they found is that the economic benefits of the Canal had really diminished by the 1960s. So the decision by the US to transfer the Canal to Panama wasn’t some benevolent generosity. It was more that the United States, at this point, really wasn’t finding it that useful. And in that post-colonial period of history, it was unseemly that the US owned the heart of another country. So there were a lot of straightforward reasons.

Was aviation the big factor in the decline, or a change in key trade routes, or…?

Aviation, the interstate highway, and the fact that rail freight became cheaper as diesel was available… Also, the West Coast of the US developed more, and there were more markets there. So the Canal became a little less important.

One of the things Americans usually don’t realise about the Canal is that when the Panamanians took it over, they ran it better. It makes more money, it’s safer, it’s more efficient. They do a better job in every way, which is hard for Americans to believe because we think we’re the best.

Well, that brings us to your last choice. Let’s talk about the Panamanian view on the Panama Canal. Please introduce us to Erased: The Untold Story Of The Panama Canal.

This is a great book to end with because it has a very different approach. It’s by a Panamanian scholar, Marixa Lasso, and she centres Panama in her story. She emphasises that the Canal wasn’t built on empty land, that it was a thriving society, crucial to the Republic of Panama, which had been densely inhabited, urbanised, very active commercially, and shaped by long histories of transportation and exchange. She looks at the impact of the Canal, and in particular, she focuses on the decision of the United States to depopulate most of the zone.

About 40,000 residents of what became the Canal Zone were expelled. For some of them, this was because the building of Gatun Lake and the dam meant that some areas were flooded and people had to leave, but most of it was not necessary. Most of it was just because the United States wanted to have much more control over the landscape. So it’s about how the imperial power, the United States, produced a whole new landscape. They had to create replacement settlements, and they had segregated communities reorganised along the corridor.

Then, on top of all of that, she’s really interesting for thinking about Panama’s place in the world. For example, she talks about the ways in which the US saw itself as modern and bringing modernity to Panama, and she looks at the ways in which Panama was already modern, and the ways that the United States messed with its sense of itself and its own modernity.

Ultimately – this is perhaps the most important thing – she connects the depopulation and the erasure of communities to erasures of memory, and the ways in which Panama itself is written out of the story of the Panama Canal.

Julie Greene

Julie Greene is a historian of United States, transnational, and global labor and immigration. She is the author of Box 25: Archival Secrets, Caribbean Workers, and the Panama Canal, which explores a set of remarkable memoirs written by canal workers (and held in Box 25 at the Library of Congress) as the starting point for considering migration, power, and silences in history. Previously, Greene authored The Canal Builders: Making America's Empire at the Panama Canal, which received the Organization of American Historians’ James A. Rawley Prize for the best book on the history of race relations.

entries.title: Booker Prize-Nominated Science Fiction Novels, recommended by Cal Flyn
entries.summary: It has just been announced that this year's winner of the Booker Prize is M. John Harrison's thought-provoking dystopian novel The End of Everything. He is, according to the Booker chief executive, the first "bona fide" sci fi writer to win fiction's biggest prize. But he is far from the first literary novelist to turn to the speculative in pursuit of their art. Our deputy editor Cal Flyn put toge
entries.content:
Speculative fiction is often used as a means of exploring contemporary issues through a prism of fantastical or science fictional storytelling. As a result, many of our greatest literary novelists have turned to futuristic or extraterrestrial scenarios in their work. Yet, as Gaby Wood, the Booker Prize’s chief executive, noted, the 2026 winner M. John Harrison is “the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide S.F. world.”

Cult favourite M. John Harrison – at 81, the oldest ever Booker Prize winner – has been writing since the 1960s, and his books are often described as “genre-defying” – reinterpreting or reworking the typical conventions of science fiction. (“A good ground rule for writing in any genre is: start with a form, then undermine its confidence in itself,” as he once told the Guardian. “Ask what it’s afraid of, what it’s trying to hide – then write that.”)

His Booker-winning book, The End of Everything, does just that; set in a near-future Kent, England, it features a beachcomber who discovers a mysterious, apparently intelligent “artifact” on the shoreline, which he must carry into the dystopian hinterlands inland – even as it grows and changes in form and nature. Writing in the Literary Review, Olivia Ho called it “a work of uncanny beauty, tender and terrifying in equal parts.”

Harrison’s science fiction pedigree may be purest, but a number of previous nominees and winners have employed science fictional aspects in their work. For example: Samantha Harvey won the 2024 Booker Prize for her slim and atmospheric novel Orbital, which is set on the International Space Station; not a traditional sci-fi novel by any means, but rather a thoughtful account of astronauts going about their daily routines and observing their home planet from space. If you read science fiction for the plot and the peril, then Orbital is not the book for you, but what it does offer is a wonderful sense of the interstellar sublime.

And for those who observe a stricter definition – never fear. We’ve put together a list of five excellent novels with strong science fiction elements that have all been nominated for the Booker Prize over the years.

 

The Sirian Experiments by Doris Lessing – shortlisted for the 1981 Booker Prize

The first science fiction novel ever to be selected by the Booker Prize judges was Doris Lessing’s The Sirian Experiments (1980). Lessing, the winner of the 2007 Nobel Prize for Literature, is most celebrated for her 1962 novel The Golden Notebook, but she also wrote a five-book sci-fi sequence, ‘Canopus in Argos,’ exploring multiple civilisations on an imagined far-future Earth. The Sirian Experiments came third in the series, and features a fascistic extraterrestrial culture fighting for control of the Earth-like planet of Shikasta.

The wildly speculative Canopus in Argos series was received with bafflement by the literary community. (The critic John Leonard complained that “I, and rational discourse, have lost a friend… to a smog of mystifications.”) Undaunted, Lessing explained in the preamble to The Sirian Experiments that she used science fiction to “put questions, both to myself and to others; to explore ideas and sociological possibilities,” although personally she preferred to use the term “space fiction” to describe her project, which drew also on Sufi ideas of cosmic evolution.

 

Oryx and Crake by Margaret Atwood – shortlisted for the 2003 Booker Prize

Margaret Atwood has been nominated for the Booker Prize no less than six times and won it twice. She made her first appearance on the shortlist back in 1986 for her landmark feminist dystopia, The Handmaid’s Tale; it’s sequel The Testaments was the joint winner in 2019 alongside Bernardine Evaristo’s Girl, Woman, Other. Both of those novels explore a nightmarish theocracy in a post-war, almost unrecognisable United States, but are not overtly science fictional in nature.

Her 2003 novel Oryx and Crake, on the other hand, is unapologetically sci-fi in form. The first book in her Maddaddam trilogy opens in a post-apocalyptic world, ruled by biotech conglomerates and featuring a gentle, genetically-engineered humanoid species known as ‘Crakers.’ In it, a figure called ‘Snowman’ ruminates on the collapse of civilisation and suspects himself to be the last surviving human as he positions himself as a caretaker to the Crakers, the creation of his brilliant former friend. It’s a dark parable warning of the dangers and deceptions of a rapaciously capitalist society.

 

Cloud Atlas by David Mitchell – shortlisted for the 2004 Booker Prize

Mitchell’s ingenious novel takes the form of six nested stories, each set in a different time period but linked in some way through recurring objects or characters. Each story starts strong, before being interrupted by the beginning of the next story until – at the midpoint – the direction changes, and the stories come to their conclusions in reverse order. (Mitchell was, he has said, inspired by Italo Calvino’s If on a winter’s night a traveller…).

Each story has its own strong character and setting: one takes the form of a colonial-era maritime journal, another a crime thriller, with all the classic mystery conventions. For our purposes, the most relevant section is the fifth strand, titled ‘An Orison of Sonmi-451’, a science fiction story about cloned slaves written in Q&A form. (The final story, ‘Sloosha’s Crossin’ an’ Eve’ry’thin’ After,’ also offers a vision of a Tolkienesque future presented in a fictional dialect, in which Sonmi-451 reappears as a local deity.) Brilliantly imaginative and cleverly structured, although bear in mind that the sci-fi element makes up only a small proportion of the full text.

 

Klara and the Sun by Kazuo Ishiguro – longlisted for the 2021 Booker Prize

Klara is an outdated model of ‘artificial friend’ – an android purchased to keep a struggling teenage girl company. Despite Klara’s excellent skills of observation and empathy, her programming prevents her from understanding certain truths about the world around her. And Josie’s mother, fearing the worst for her sickly daughter, has unsettling plans for her continuation should the worst happen.

Klara and the Sun – which was recently adapted for the screen by Taika Waititi, albeit to poor reviews  – is an unusually sweet-natured take on the dystopian novel, in which our view of an unsettling, technologically advanced future is tempered by seeing it through the eyes of a benevolent robot. “I was drawn to a narrator with peculiar limitations of vision, as well as outstanding abilities to observe and learn quickly about the human world,” the author has explained. “An extreme outsider at the same time child-like and sophisticated. Through her eyes it would feel natural to ask big questions like: What’s special about humans? Are humans fundamentally lonely? What do humans mean when they say they love one another?”

 

In Ascension by Martin MacInnes – longlisted for the 2023 Booker Prize

Leigh, a marine biologist with a specialism in algae, takes up a position on board a deep-sea submarine exploring an ocean trench deeper than any previously studied. But all is not quite as it seems – uncanny things are happening on board, and the mission is proceeding according to a secret agenda. Leigh’s research ultimately earns her a new job for a space agency, studying algae as a sustainable food source for ultra-long-distance travel. But as her first major mission approaches, Leigh realises she must choose between a life of interplanetary adventure and supporting her sister with the care for their ailing mother.

“I’m exploring interconnectedness because it’s vital and relatively absent from English language fiction, too much of which draws a world in which humanity is walled off from the rest of creation, as if we were entirely self-involved, made from some other, more rarefied kind of stuff,” explained the author in an interview on the Booker website. Despite dramatic plot points, the result is a long, eerie and somewhat slow-moving novel. As a result, it has been divisive among sci-fi fans – especially those who went in hoping for a rapid-fire eco-thriller. In Ascension is for those who like their science fiction literary, and as much about human relationships as extraterrestrial forces.

entries.title: The Best History Books of 2026: The Wolfson History Prize, recommended by Helen McCarthy
entries.summary: The Wolfson History Prize is awarded every year to history books that wed scholarly originality to popular accessibility. Here, historian Helen McCarthy talks us through the 2026 shortlist, with books covering everything from 7th-century BC Mesopotamia to the 16th-century German Peasants’ War and the postwar history of Liverpool. This interview appeared first on Five Books.
entries.content:
Before we talk about the books, can you say a bit about how you got down to these six? Was it an easy process? Were they the standout candidates, or was there a lot of head scratching?

There was quite a lot of debate and discussion, but I think that all the judges are really happy and excited with the final six. We all come with our different interests and areas of expertise, and all bring our own particular preferences to the table. But then we’re able to really share our thinking and what excited us about the books that we’ve chosen. It was a really stimulating conversation. It was just so interesting and illuminating to hear what my colleagues thought about the books that I’d read, and how, in many cases, we responded quite differently to them.

How many books did you have to get through on the long list?

The way it works is that publishers can nominate titles, and then the judges can call in any books that we are interested in. So I think the final full tally was something like 140.

Wow!

So, yes, that’s quite a lot of books. But then we whittled those down fairly dramatically to about 30, and there was a much more intense debate and process of reflection on those.

Let’s start with The Boundless Deep: Young Tennyson, Science and the Crisis of Belief by Richard Holmes. This is a biography of Alfred, Lord Tennyson and focuses on his interest in the scientific world of the early-to-mid 19th century, doesn’t it?

Yes. This is literary biography, and written by Richard Holmes, who’s an absolute master of the genre. As you would expect, it’s an incredibly well-written book. It really keeps you hooked and engaged, and one of the things that we’re always looking for is books that are just great writing—writing that really excites, engages, and holds the attention of the reader. There’s absolutely no question that Holmes does that. But it’s also a biography which sets Tennyson in time and place, and tells us something about this particular moment in the early-to-mid 19th century, when artistic expression and literary creation were absolutely fundamentally entangled with scientific discovery and new ideas about the universe, about archaeology, about the origins of the planet. All of these new discoveries were really exciting for Tennyson, but also discombobulating.

They caused him to question his religious faith and provoked extraordinary levels of anxiety about the future of the planet and about the extinction of the human race. All of this is really important for understanding his poetry and his life. Holmes weaves this all together really brilliantly.

For me, the key takeaway was just how, for early Victorians, it really would have made no sense to think about the arts and the sciences separately. The two were absolutely part of the same world of knowledge and discovery. And it really reminds us, when we are so siloed in the way we think about academic disciplines and fields of knowledge, to remember that this wouldn’t have made sense even 150 years ago.

Next up is Vanished: The Unnatural History of Extinction by Sadiah Qureshi.

I really loved this book. I thought it was just so original in its subject matter and how it frames its theme. It’s a book about extinction, and actually, there are interesting connections here with some of the ideas that Tennyson was engaging with in the early 19th century.

It’s about how the idea of extinction develops not just into a scientific understanding of the natural world, but also a political ideology or an idea that has very important consequences for the way that European empires conducted themselves. It brings together histories of the natural world—histories of knowledge about nature and of fossils, dinosaurs and animal species—with understandings of how human societies are classified and belong to this story of progress, but also how they are touched by ideas about vulnerability and future extinction.

It’s a very clever book in the way it brings together histories of science, empire, race, and the environment, and it’s also really engaged in ethical questions about the preservation and display of human remains, for example, and questions of repair and redress, where indigenous peoples have been dispossessed of their land. It’s all done with a real authority, but also an emotional and moral engagement. It’s a book that really challenges you to think about what we owe the past and what we owe the natural world.

There’s a wonderful bit at the end where Qureshi asks: which species would you mourn the loss of? Maybe your favourite animal? Well, actually, that animal may not be here forever because so many of these—what she calls lifeways—have disappeared from the planet. It’s a very thoughtful but also thought-provoking book, which is also brilliantly researched and wonderfully wide-ranging. She takes us to Australia, North America, Paris, South Kensington. We go everywhere in this wonderful book.

Does it cover a particular period? It obviously has a contemporary side to it, but how wide-ranging is it over time?

It’s mostly 18th century onwards because the story begins with the Enlightenment moment and new ways of thinking about science and the natural world, and new systems of knowledge formation. She’s particularly interested in museums of natural history, and how these are growing up at the same time as European empires are conquering and plundering other parts of the world.

And are there particular important protagonists in the book? Does it have its heroes or anti-heroes?

No one is entirely heroic. There are lots of interesting individuals who are part of the story. One of the really powerful stories is that of Shanawdithit, who was an indigenous woman, a member of the Beothuk people of Newfoundland, and Qureshi tells the story of how the Beothuk were essentially destroyed and rendered extinct by European colonialists. Shanawdithit was an extraordinary woman in the early 19th century whose sketches and drawings are pretty much the only source that we have that was produced by an indigenous woman from this period. So it’s a moment where we can actually see the hand of an indigenous woman in the archive. Most of the archive—and Qureshi is very clear about this and tries to read against the grain—is produced by ethnographers, scientists, European colonialists, the archives of government.

Let’s move on to Summer of Fire and Blood: The German Peasants’ War by Lyndal Roper. She’s a biographer of Martin Luther as well, isn’t she?

She is, and this is a companion volume in a way to her biography of Luther, insofar as she’s still looking at Reformation-era Germany. But Summer of Fire and Blood de-centres Luther and tells a different story about the Reformation, its origins and what gave it its particular character. The Peasants’ War took place in 1524-26, and the peasants who fought were inspired by the ideas of Luther. Luther talked about spiritual freedom, but the peasants reinterpreted or adapted this idea to mean freedom from lordship and freedom to enjoy the resources of the land and to be equal in the eyes of God and in God’s natural creation. It’s a book that really places the thoughts, the motivations, the feelings, and the dreams of the peasants themselves at the centre, even though it’s quite tricky to reconstruct all of that from the sources, which have been mostly produced by the lords, who ultimately won out.

I knew very little about the German Peasants’ War before I read this book. It’s one of those big, chunky, essay topics—what caused the German peasants’ uprising of 1524-6? There have been lots of Marxist-inflected explanations, which have looked at the systems of economic production and ownership of the land. That was very much a legacy of the 19th-century scholarship.

But what Roper is saying is that we have to recreate the peasants’ world. We have to understand their relationship with the land, with the landscape, with the weather, with animals, with the natural resources that shaped their everyday lives and on which they rely to live. We also need to understand the forms of community and brotherhood that were facilitated by this uprising. Roper is very good on gender, showing how this is an uprising that is led by men and is driven by a very powerful ideology of brotherhood, but in which you can still recover the roles that women are playing.

What about the relationship to the Reformation? Luther famously wrote a tract, didn’t he, against the peasant uprising. He was appalled by it. But was he the cause of it as well?

Yes, I think that’s what Roper’s saying. Some of Luther’s ideas about freedom and his critique of the monasteries and so on absolutely inspired this uprising. But he ultimately says, ‘Oh, I didn’t actually mean it that way. Freedom, yes, but not like that!’ And Luther essentially sides with the lords, which for Roper helps to explain why the Reformation ends up becoming quite a conservative Reformation rather than a socially radical one. So there’s a sense of this being a moment of possibility, of contingency, when the Reformation could have looked rather different if the outcome of the peasants’ revolt had been different. She’s trying to recreate that sense of things being on a knife edge. This is a moment when the vision of what the Reformation is going to be is up for grabs.

Were there trials or some kind of great reckoning afterwards where the peasants had their say because they were in court, or is there nothing left like that?

They’re mostly slaughtered by the armies of the lords. The huge violence and bloodshed with which the war ends is something that is conveyed very vividly. Roper, as you may know from some of her previous books, sometimes uses psychoanalytic ideas in a very skilful way to try and capture that sense of trauma and how there’s a kind of lingering effect over decades, perhaps even centuries.

There’s an interesting coincidence where some of the areas that witnessed a witch craze in the early 17th century were areas where there had been a lot of death and slaughter at the end of the Peasants’ War. And Roper just lightly suggests that maybe there’s some kind of lingering trauma. Maybe there’s a relationship between these two things.

Let’s move on to Liverpool: A Story of Britain by Sam Wetherell.

This book is just terrific. This book is more in my field as a modern British historian, and you look at it and you think, ‘Oh, it’s a book about Liverpool. Well, that’s one city, and it only covers 1945 onwards. Isn’t that a little bit narrow?’ But it really isn’t because what Wetherell is doing is using Liverpool as a case study, as a lens through which to think more broadly about the processes that are remaking British society and Britain’s place in the world in the later 20th century and into the present. It’s a very politically engaged book. He has quite a fierce authorial voice. It’s very sharp and bracing in the way it’s written. Wetherell is a really wonderful writer, and he develops a very clear argument about obsolescence. He talks about Liverpool being a kind of prophecy for what happens when the forces of global capitalism buffet a place and render it obsolete, along with the people who live there and the factories and wharves and shipyards that once served as the centre of a maritime empire and a thriving manufacturing industry. Suddenly, all of this looks no longer fit for purpose. What do you do with a place like that? And what do you do with the people in it when they no longer seem to be part of history’s forward march? They seem to be left behind.

It is a book about the specificities of Liverpool, but there are all sorts of things in it that speak to larger histories of deindustrialisation and the transition to a post-industrial economy, mass immigration and multiculturalism, racial violence and resistance, changing gender roles, the family, childhood, domestic life and the fabric of people’s homes and streets. There’s a huge amount in there. If you’re interested in Britain, you’re going to be interested in this book.

When does it kick off? Does it start in the 1980s when all these problems really crystallised, or does he start before then?

He starts in 1945, although there is a chapter where he gives you a quick potted history of Liverpool because, obviously, the legacy of the slave trade and its place in the maritime empire is really important. He fills that in quite quickly. Then we move on to the period from 1945. It’s a rise and fall narrative in so far as there is a period in the 1950s and 1960s where there’s some optimism. It looks as though industry is booming. New suburban housing estates are being built for these quite well-paid white working-class manual workers. The Beatles appear and storm the world, and it seems as though Liverpool is on the up, but that changes very quickly. It’s a story of this moment. It’s almost as though there are particular political choices that are holding at bay some of the forces that, in the 1970s and 1980s, decimate industry.

There’s a wonderful section about the containerization of shipping and how the creation of this new transportation technology just destroys, pretty much at a stroke, the whole purpose of the docklands in Liverpool, which then fall into disuse and dilapidation. Then they are rejuvenated by a kind of heritage and cultural industry in the 1990s, and gentrified.

He’s really interesting on how what he calls the ruins of that previous era, of a political economy rooted in manufacturing industry and social democratic politics, fades away, but leaves these physical ruins, these remains that you have to do something with—you turn them into a museum or converted luxury flats.

Let’s move on to The Library of Ancient Wisdom, Mesopotamia and the Making of History by Selena Wisnom.

I came to this book essentially with zero knowledge of Assyriology and of cuneiform tablets. I’d walk past them in the British Museum without any understanding of just how wonderful they are. This book was just utterly compelling and it made me think: what have I been missing all of this time?

This is about the first writing system, when human beings began to write things down, and it’s a very clever book because it focuses on a particular collection of cuneiform tablets, 30,000 of them, that were collected by King Ashurbanipal in his library in Nineveh in the seventh century BC. He was a kind of philosopher-king who was really interested in knowledge and collecting, and also in the past. He wanted to bring all of this knowledge together and preserve it in his library. And the reason that we still have access to this is because the library burned down in 612 BC and the fire baked the clay tablets, hardening them, which meant that they survived and could then be discovered thousands of years later by archaeologists.

Mesopotamian civilization goes on for about 2,000 years, but Wisnom is looking at a particular phase of it in the sixth and seventh centuries BC, and really wants us to look at it from as many different angles as possible. There are chapters on religion and belief, chapters on medicine and healing, on trade and farming. There is a chapter on family and marriage and children and education. So you get a real sense of what Assyrians believed, how they saw the world, how they lived their lives. She’s astonishingly accomplished to be able to read these tablets. I’m in awe of her abilities! And she’s also a wonderful writer. Each chapter opens with a little scene written in the present tense which takes the reader into the world of the Assyrians, helping to make it live vividly before the text moves on to develop the particular theme of the chapter in a more analytical way. It’s a really wonderful book to read.

Do the tablets cover all those different areas, or is she drawing on broader archaeological work?

It’s primarily based on the tablets.

Next up is Silence of the Gods: the Untold History of Europe’s Last Pagans by Francis Young. Is this a story of Eastern Europe?

Yes. The main areas that it focuses on are the Baltics and this geographically very remote strip, which was quite difficult for Christian missionaries to get to. But they do get there, and this is a story really about what happens when they do. There are several things that are very thought-provoking about this book. First of all, you think Christianity had swept Europe by the medieval period, and Europe was essentially Christendom by that point. From then on, all religious battles were going to be carried out within Christianity rather than between Christianity and pre-Christian religions. Obviously, encounters with Islam and encounters with Judaism are an important part of the history of European religion, but encounters with pre-Christian religions have not really been part of that story. Young is trying to bring these pre-Christian religions together and write them back into that story of European Christianity. Again, these are things I knew nothing about. I’d never heard of the Mordvins, the Chuvashes, the Udmurts. I really just didn’t know that these pre-Christian communities were still very much part of Europe’s religious life well into the 19th century.

This goes right into the 19th century, does it?

Yes. It’s a very scholarly book. Of all these books, it’s the most scholarly one. They’re all based on brilliant research, but this is the one where that research is most to the fore, because Young’s really trying to show how the encounter with Christianity is transforming these pre-Christian religions. One of the big ideas of the book is to do with how we routinely talk about ‘pagan religion’ and ‘pagans,’ suggesting something very ancient, static, primitive and unchanging, when actually there’s a really dynamic story in play about how these pre-Christian religions are changed and evolve and adapt to some kind of coexistence with Christianity.

Young offers some interesting thoughts at the end of the book, where he talks about what we might take from this history for our own religiously pluralistic societies. Do they offer any clues as to how different belief systems can coexist? There was quite a lot of violence, coercion and oppression of these pre-Christian religions, so there are lessons to be learned from that as well.

Did these pre-Christian religions share particular characteristics or beliefs, or are they very diverse in their creeds and practices?

They are very diverse. Young does talk about animism as being a shared characteristic—the idea that objects have supernatural qualities. This is something that a lot of these pre-Christian religions hold in common, and which Christian missionaries don’t quite know what to do with because it’s so far outside their understanding of the spiritual aspects of the world.

He also talks about magic and sorcery as something that Christian observers often read into these pre-Christian religions. They interpret their rites as forms of sorcery or magic. But they do seem to be very diverse.

And when or how did they finally get eliminated? It sounds like that’s the story of the book. What happened to these last pagan religions?

Again, it’s quite a complex picture. In all of these places, you still find people who identify with these religions or systems of belief and may continue to practice some aspects of their rituals and traditions, but often coexisting with Christianity. So it’s a story of adaptation and coexistence as much as it is of elimination and suppression.
